SOCIAL MEDIA BUSTING CRIME

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Social Media is fast becoming a crime-busting tool – internationally and here in SA.

Summary:
Social media sites provide people with an easy way to stay connected with family members and friends, but these sites can also serve as a helpful crime-solving tool.

South African investigators are using social media to track down criminals and get them behind bars.


Further information:
With social media, it’s very difficult not to leave some kind of trace of your existence – someone, somewhere will recognise you.

Law enforcement personnel are using social media tools in increasingly unique and effective ways, from locating criminals and evidence to communicating directly with the community about public safety matters.

INTERNATIONALLY – LEXIS NEXIS STUDY
A 2013 study found that using social media in criminal investigation is becoming a global trend that is leading to the successful prosecution of criminal cases.

ONLINE VIDEOS
Posting videos of criminal activities help investigators locate criminals. PI Warren Lamont runs an investigation firm with a very active social media presence. He says within an hour of posting clips that are shared thousands of times and are almost guaranteed to deliver a lead with that first hour. He posts videos of armed robberies, cash-in-transit heists and hijackings – all crimes that have spiked in last year’s crime stats.

People find a sense of community in the cyber world and are keen to unite for a cause in the realm of social media and are quick to respond to expose criminals in an effort to get justice.

HOW INVESTIGATORS USE SOCIAL MEDIA
Identifying Suspects
Not only do officials use social media to gather evidence on suspect behavior, but they use it to find who their suspects are. As with the Boston bombing during the 2013 Boston Marathon, police officials used pictures and videos from witnesses’ social media profiles to help identify the bombers.

Identifying Links between Gang Members
When police are tracking down a gang, social media plays a huge role in identifying who is involved in the gang activity.

GOING UNDERCOVER ON FACEBOOK
A more controversial approach to getting information from social networks is going undercover online -- creating fake profiles to befriend suspects. Facebook, where almost 9% of accounts are believed to be fakes or duplicates, frowns on this practice, however. While these fake accounts may violate a social network's rules, they are not illegal. And evidence collected in this way can still hold up in court.

LEGAL CHALLENGES
Police and prosecutors are not as keen on social media posts – arguing witness testimony is compromised. But PI’s argue that suspects are arrested can clearly be linked to the CCTV footage and that the witness testimoney should become secondary.

RECENT SA STUDY – nice hook with stats
The Victims of Crime Survey released this week was conducted by the Statistician General, was conducted in conjunction with the SAPS and based on a national representative sample size of approximately 30 000 households between the period 2011 to 2014/15.
The main objective of the study was to explore the factors which increase or decrease the risk of "social fabric related or selected contact crimes" in South Africa.
The majority of murders comminted in Urban Settlements are by people aged between 15 and 34, while murders in urban metros are commited by people between the the ages of 34 and 50.
HOW WE DO IT
We can find a specific case that was solved recently to trace the steps, from the post to the lead to catching the crook. We look at the psycology behind social media crime busters.

Press Release:


Social Media Busting Crime
Could social media platforms be an ideal tool to track down and arrest criminals? Carte Blanche meets investigators using online platforms to connect communities and make it impossible for even the most cunning criminals to hide.


Script:


STRUCTURE SOCIAL MEDIA & CRIME

VO: As Social Media infiltrates every aspect of our daily lives, it’s fast becoming a powerful crime-solving tool - with law enforcers turning to social media to out criminals and get them behind bars.

LINK: Social media really is a game changer when it comes to fighting crime, unlike a poster in your local shopping centres, there are literally hundreds of thousands of pairs of eyes looking for people and the net closes in fast.

VO: Today, 8 in 10 American law enforcement professionals use social media as an investigative tool. Crowdsourcing in the Internet age has taken the public's involvement in solving crimes to a whole new level.

The 2013 Boston Marathon Bombing is a prime example – law enforcement officials used pictures and videos from witnesses’ social media profiles to help identify and capture the bombers.

Authorities scrutinised images posted before the explosion to pinpoint and identify the suspects, then a global online search was launched with suspects pictures shared and reposted hundreds of thousands of times.

South African investigators are picking up on this growing global trend.

PI Warren Lamont posts crime alerts as they come in and shares videos almost daily – he says this is delivering results.

This video was shared 754 times and reached over 800 000 people.

The car’s licence plates are fake, but the suspects have been identified and are being tracked down.

WARREN: We’re getting a lot of people coming back to us with credible info // someone’s phoned in said, this is this guy, this is where he lives, I know him and he’s a known criminal and we get results that way.

VO: It’s all about networking – getting all the different roleplayers to work together.

A crime alert was shared on Warren’s page.

It was reposted at least 200 times and just hours later – authorities were closing in on the suspects – this video shows the chase.

WARREN: What we have here is private security industry as well as the general public, as well as SAPS all working together.

WARREN: There’s the SAPS chopper, the particular vehicle here is a security company, you’ll see the suspect vehicle on the left – he knew rather stop than be disabled. And this is where they apprehend these particular suspects.

VO: There are examples of when crime related posts have reached millions of social media users - making it a very powerful investigative tool.

LINK: The real power of social media isn’t just the fact that any body can see it, but it’s the speed with which people share, repost and tag others – information spreads like wild fire.

VO: This Be On the Look Out post was picked up by an armed response team in Alberton – the information was circulated to all their reaction teams and guards.

TYRONE: We received a call from one of the guards in our shopping centre, requesting back up with regards to the vehicle and the armed robbery that was taking place. We had a lookout for the vehicle, so everything was confirmed.

VO: Reaction units raced to the scene – an armed robbery was in progress.

TYRONE: the guys tried their luck here at our centre, and we were fortunate enough to catch the guys before they could exit the centre after they committed a robbery at The Hub.

VO: Five suspects were arrested and all stolen goods were recovered. And, they were linked to the incident on Warren’s post.

When it comes posting crime related info - it’s even more critical to get your facts right before clicking to share. It can be very dangerous when some media and the public opt to value speed over accuracy, using social media to spread incorrect, unverified information.

Recently, in the Western Cape, an elderly woman was wrongfully accused of being a kidnapper. The social media post was shared over 28 000 times.

While the original post has been removed. The woman in question has demanded a public apology and has threatened to take legal action saying her reputation has been damaged.

Warren says they have never compromised a case, but the wheels of justice turns slowly, even with video evidence.

WARREN: most of them have resulted in a criminal record being brought up against the person. The judicial system is quite tough // a lot of the cases in general have been thrown out due to a lack of evidence or keep going on the roll, postponed, postponed…

VO: Posting clips, may not always lead to arrests and convictions – but outing criminals is always invaluable says Warren.

This clip was of a cross-pavement Cash in Transit Robbery in Durban.

Although no workable leads have materialised via the post, it has been viewed over 85000 times.

WARREN: We have been told that oh no, the hijackers or the criminals may be watching your page. We actually want them to know that we’ve got their footage, we’ve got people alerting us to their whereabouts.

VO: Warren believes we can beat crime – if people just become more aware - if you see something, say something.

WARREN: I think people are tired of crime in South Africa and they are basically wanting to put an end to it.


PROMOS

10 SECOND PROMO
VO: Social media is a game changer when it comes to fighting crime - with literally hundreds of thousands of pairs of eyes looking for criminal suspects, the net closes in fast.


15 SECOND PROMO
VO: Social Media is becoming a global crime-solving tool helping to out criminals and getting them behind bars.

WARREN: We’re getting a lot of people coming back to us with credible info // most of them have resulted in a criminal record being brought up against the person.


15 SECOND PROMO
VO: Reposted Crime alerts are reaching millions of social media users – connecting a network of crime busters closing in on suspects.

WARREN: What we have here is private security industry as well as the general public, as well as SAPS all working together.
